title: When Error Mitigation Makes Things Worse:Budget-Aware Evaluation, Extrapolation Failure,and the Calibration Trust Boundary

paper.title: When Error Mitigation Makes Things Worse: Budget-Aware Evaluation, Extrapolation Failure, and the Calibration Trust Boundary
paper.abstract: Abstract Error mitigation is expected to turn noisy quantum measurements into more useful estimates. We show that it can instead amplify error. Under control-offset miscalibration, the evaluated unconstrained zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) estimators are worse than no mitigation on 38–63% of simulated instances and produce extreme tail errors. A small IBM Heron study finds worsening on 80–88% of 18 instances across two depths, with mean error 3.0 3.0 – 4.1 × 4.1\times the raw error. In simulation, the median changes little, so median-only monitoring misses the failures. We then compare methods at the same online shot budget per evaluation and report offline training cost separately. After that cost is amortized, a budget-conditioned neural corrector occupies the low-budget end of the simulated accuracy–cost frontier and falls back to the raw estimate when an ensemble disagrees; its hardware transfer remains unsuccessful. Finally, we treat provider-reported calibration as an input that is not bound to the execution-time device state. A white-box projected-gradient stress test on this metadata increases the corrector’s error 8.1 × 8.1\times within the feature ranges used for training and evades the disagreement monitor on half of the worsened cases. Together, the results connect budget-aware evaluation, tail risk, and calibration integrity in near-term quantum learning pipelines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Variational quantum algorithms such as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are leading candidates for near-term quantum advantage, but their expectation-value estimates are biased by device noise [ 24 , 9 , 4 , 28 ] . Error mitigation aims to remove this bias without the qubit overhead of error correction [ 27 , 7 ] , and in practice it is the component that quantum machine learning pipelines trust to turn noisy hardware output into usable numbers. The most widely used technique, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), amplifies noise by gate folding and extrapolates the measurements back to the zero-noise limit [ 27 , 20 , 14 , 16 ] . Learning-based methods such as Clifford data regression (CDR) instead fit a noisy-to-ideal map on classically simulable circuits run on the same device [ 11 , 26 ] . This paper examines that trust from two directions that are often studied separately. The first is reliability : does a corrected answer improve on the raw one at an affordable quantum budget, and how badly does it fail when its assumptions break? The second is security : what information does the mitigation layer trust, and how can an adversary manipulate it? On reliability, the usual comparison hides a first-order distinction. Methods are compared at a fixed, generous number of shots per circuit execution , yet they need very different numbers of executions per estimate: ZNE three to five, CDR more than thirty per target circuit, a neural model trained offline exactly one. Inside a VQA loop that evaluates thousands of parameter settings under a per-iteration shot budget, these multiplicities decide which method is usable, not the accuracy at unlimited shots. Bultrini et al. [6] made the budget axis explicit for classical methods; we extend it to learned mitigation and make the budget an input of the model itself. Figure 1 summarizes the study. We contribute three pieces of evidence. First, we map the tail-risk boundary of ZNE under coherent offset error and reproduce the failure pattern in a small real-hardware study. Second, we compare raw execution, learned correction, ZNE, and CDR at the same online shot budget, while keeping the learned model’s offline simulation cost visible. Third, we formalize provider-reported calibration as an execution-unbound input and evaluate a projected-gradient metadata attack. The learned corrector is a test case rather than an architectural contribution: CDR remains more accurate when its larger online budget is affordable. Figure 1: Study design. Four mitigation pipelines share one online shot budget and a frozen noise snapshot. Three simulated regimes and a small IBM Heron run support the accuracy–cost, ZNE tail-risk, and metadata-attack analyses.

sections.heading: Classical mitigation.
sections.text: ZNE [ 27 , 20 ] assumes the bias varies smoothly with a controllable noise-scale factor; digital implementations amplify noise by unitary folding [ 14 ] , with headline demonstrations at the 100-qubit scale [ 16 ] ; its reliability, however, is contingent on the extrapolation ansatz matching the actual noise response, a sensitivity we quantify in Section 6.2 . Probabilistic error cancellation and virtual distillation trade unbiasedness or stronger suppression for exponential sampling or additional quantum cost [ 27 , 30 , 15 , 17 ] . CDR [ 11 ] fits a linear noisy-to-ideal regression on near-Clifford circuits executed on the device, paying tens of executions per target circuit but inheriting robustness to noise structure because it calibrates on the device as it actually is; Strikis et al. [26] extend the idea with learning-based protocols. Bultrini et al. [6] show that low-cost methods win at small total shot budgets, while data-hungry methods win at large budgets. Our protocol builds on that observation.

sections.heading: Learned mitigation.
sections.text: Neural networks have been used to reconstruct observables from noisy quantum data [ 29 ] , mitigate errors in quantum simulation [ 3 ] , and predict ideal expectation values from noisy values and circuit structure [ 21 , 8 ] . Noise-agnostic [ 22 ] and per-circuit-adaptive [ 1 ] variants have also been validated on small hardware experiments. Prior work rarely places learned mitigation and classical baselines on the same online shot budget, and the integrity of calibration inputs remains underexplored. We focus on those two gaps.

sections.heading: Quantum computing security.
sections.text: A growing literature attacks quantum computing at the hardware and controller layers: crosstalk-based fault injection in multi-programmed NISQ devices [ 2 ] , crosstalk side channels that reveal a co-tenant’s circuit [ 10 ] , and power side channels on classical controllers [ 12 ] . Adversarial robustness of quantum classifiers has been studied at the model level [ 23 ] . Blind and verifiable quantum computation addresses delegated computation cryptographically [ 5 , 13 ] , although its costs remain impractical for NISQ clouds. We study the classical mitigation layer between these settings and the execution-unbound calibration metadata it consumes.

sections.heading: 3 Threat model: provider calibration as a trust boundary
sections.text: Error mitigation is usually analyzed as a numerical problem. In a cloud pipeline it is also security-relevant because the user cannot independently verify the execution-time device state. Provider-reported calibration is authenticated as provider data, but it is not cryptographically bound to the physical process that produced a particular set of counts. We therefore treat it as a trust boundary and study how reliability failures transfer to an adversarial setting.

sections.heading: Setting.
sections.text: A mitigated pipeline spans three parties: the user , who compiles circuits and performs classical post-processing; the provider , who executes them on a typically multi-tenant QPU and publishes gate errors, T 1 / T 2 T_{1}/T_{2} , readout asymmetries, and drift statistics; and co-tenants on the same device. The user cannot independently verify the measured counts at scale or confirm that the published snapshot describes the device during execution. Blind and verifiable quantum computation [ 5 , 13 ] address a different integrity problem and remain impractical for the NISQ setting considered here.

sections.heading: The boundary.
sections.text: Each mitigation method trusts information that the user cannot independently verify. ZNE assumes folding scales the relevant device noise, CDR assumes its near-Clifford circuits sample the same channel as the target, and a learned corrector consumes published calibration directly as features 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} . The dependencies differ, but all sit below the user’s line of visibility.

sections.heading: A1: Calibration spoofing.
sections.text: A dishonest or compromised provider, or an attacker in the metadata path, falsifies calibration while executing circuits honestly. Against NEM this is direct input poisoning. The feature ablation of Section 6.4 shows that removing 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} triples MAE, so the controlled features are also the ones the model relies on. The sim-to-real study of Appendix C is a benign preview: a model trained under mischaracterized calibration overcorrects by 94% at five layers.

sections.heading: A2: Mitigation-aware coherent bias injection.
sections.text: An adversary with access to a calibration routine or controller [ 12 ] can choose a control offset δ \delta to increase post-mitigation error. Section 6.2 sweeps δ \delta over the range used by our noise model. For ZNE, mean error grows and 38–63% of instances become worse, while the median remains near the raw baseline. A median-only dashboard would miss this tail. The small hardware run in Section 6.3 shows that the same failure pattern can arise from ordinary device behavior, without deliberate injection.

sections.heading: A3: Co-tenant crosstalk adversaries.
sections.text: The device-layer literature demonstrates that a co-tenant can inject faults [ 2 ] and observe side channels [ 10 ] through crosstalk on multi-programmed hardware. Our stochastic-correlated regime is an illustrative proxy for this setting, not a calibrated reproduction of a specific attack. In that proxy, ZNE is worse than the raw estimate on 44–61% of instances, while the learned corrector improves the mean by 61–68% (Table 5 ).

sections.heading: Fail-safe posture and detection.
sections.text: The learned model predicts a residual correction rather than an extrapolated observable. Its outputs are not formally bounded, but the largest observed errors remain below the raw worst case in every evaluated cell. A seed-ensemble disagreement rule adds a zero-quantum-cost monitor: large disagreement returns the raw value. This is an empirical safeguard, not a robustness guarantee.

sections.heading: A PGD attack on the calibration channel.
sections.text: We test A1/A2 directly. Holding the measurement and circuit features fixed, we run projected gradient descent on the five calibration features inside an L ∞ L_{\infty} ball equal to half of each feature’s training range. On miscal n = 8 n{=}8 (150 instances), the attack raises mean error from 0.008 to 0.067 and worsens every correction (Table 6 ). At a threshold set to the 95th percentile of clean disagreement, the monitor flags half of these cases. The result is a white-box stress test of the modeled metadata range. Black-box transfer, detector-aware attacks, and empirical calibration tolerances are left to future work.

In deployment, 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} comes from the provider channel in Section 3 .

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: Figure 6 (Appendix D ) shows the model. Two multilayer-perceptron encoders embed the feature groups: the circuit encoder maps 𝐱 c \mathbf{x}_{c} through hidden widths [ 128,256 ] [128,256] to a 128-dimensional embedding, and the noise encoder maps 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} through width 64 to a 64-dimensional embedding. The embeddings are concatenated with the measured value and passed through an output network of widths [ 256,512,256 ] [256,512,256] (LayerNorm, GELU, dropout 0.15 0.15 ) that predicts a residual correction added to the input estimate. The standard configuration has 428K parameters; Section 6.4 shows accuracy is insensitive to capacity over a 5 × 5\times range, so the capacity is generous rather than necessary.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: The model minimizes Huber loss with AdamW for 75 epochs, about five minutes on a CPU workstation at the sizes studied. Training pairs ( ⟨ H ⟩ ^ noisy , 𝐱 c , 𝐱 n , ⟨ H ⟩ ideal ) (\widehat{\langle H\rangle}_{\mathrm{noisy}},\mathbf{x}_{c},\mathbf{x}_{n},\langle H\rangle_{\mathrm{ideal}}) are generated in simulation. Parameters and noise realizations are sampled per example, the input is an S S -shot estimate, and the label is an exact noiseless value. Exact labels restrict training to classically simulable sizes.

sections.heading: Budget conditioning.
sections.text: We condition training on the shot-noise scale so that one model serves every deployment budget. Each training example draws its shot count S S log-uniformly from 2 8 2^{8} to 2 16 2^{16} , samples the noisy input at that S S , and appends 1 / S 1/\sqrt{S} to 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} . The network thereby learns how much of the input fluctuation is measurement noise versus learnable bias, so no retraining is needed across budgets.

sections.heading: Costs and break-even.
sections.text: The reported model uses 4,400 simulated training pairs per device family and noise regime. This offline simulation cost is not charged to the online Pareto curves. Inference adds one classical forward pass to one quantum execution. If the same training set were collected on device, its QPU cost would break even with CDR after 142 target evaluations and with ZNE after 1,467–2,200 evaluations (Appendix B ). Classical baselines use mitiq 1.0 [ 19 ] .

sections.text: Three regimes span the noise-structure spectrum: • Stochastic device noise : per-instance profiles with depolarizing gate errors, thermal relaxation, and asymmetric readout. This is the regime where smooth noise scaling is most plausible. • Stochastic-correlated noise : adds gate-error fluctuations and correlated Z ​ Z ZZ crosstalk as a proxy for co-tenant interference. • Coherent miscalibration : models control-offset error [ 18 ] . sections.heading: Fairness protocol.
sections.text: Each test instance freezes one device snapshot. The raw measurement, NEM input, every ZNE fold point, and every CDR training circuit are S S -shot estimates under that snapshot; baseline failures abort the run. ZNE uses mitiq’s Richardson, exponential, and adaptive-exponential factories with global folding at scales { 1 , 2 , 3 } \{1,2,3\} ; CDR uses 31 near-Clifford circuits. We report 150 instances per configuration (100 for budget sweeps), paired t t -tests, and both means and medians because extrapolation is heavy-tailed.

sections.heading: 6.1 The equal-online-budget Pareto frontier
sections.text: Figure 2: Equal-online-budget comparison at n = 8 n=8 (100 instances; median | | error | | , IQR shaded). Each method splits the same inference budget B B across its required executions (Table 1 ); NEM’s offline simulation cost is reported separately. NEM is below the raw baseline at B ≤ 2 14 B\leq 2^{14} in both regimes, CDR crosses over at the largest budget, and ZNE medians track the raw line while its mean diverges. Figure 2 compares online inference after the learned model has been trained; Table 4 reports every value. Under coherent miscalibration, NEM reduces mean error by 72–81% across B = 2 10 B=2^{10} – 2 16 2^{16} . CDR rises from + 23 % +23\% at B = 2 10 B=2^{10} to + 84 % +84\% at B = 2 16 B=2^{16} and overtakes NEM at the largest budget. Both ZNE variants are negative at nearly every budget in this regime. The lone exception, adaptive ZNE at B = 2 14 B=2^{14} , has a + 7 % +7\% mean improvement but a median near the raw baseline. Under stochastic device noise, NEM is the only positive method at B ≤ 2 14 B\leq 2^{14} ( + 11 +11 to + 20 % +20\% ), while CDR turns positive at B = 2 16 B=2^{16} ( + 47 % +47\% ). These are online comparisons; Section 4 and Appendix B report the offline training cost. The practical advantage therefore depends on reuse. A learned corrector is attractive when one trained model serves many parameter settings; CDR is preferable when its larger per-target budget is affordable or reuse is limited.

sections.heading: 6.2 When extrapolation fails, and how badly
sections.text: Figure 3: Median | | error | | versus miscalibration strength δ \delta at n = 8 n=8 (80 instances per point, 8,192 shots per execution). ZNE medians coincide with the unmitigated baseline at every δ \delta ; NEM matches CDR at small δ \delta at 1 / 32 1/32 the quantum cost and declines smoothly as the unlearnable coherent share grows. Figure 3 sweeps δ \delta from 0 to 0.08 rad over a fixed stochastic background. ZNE’s median improvement never exceeds + 2 % +2\% , including at δ = 0 \delta=0 . The remaining bias there is dominated by readout error, which gate folding does not amplify. Mean error grows sharply with δ \delta ; exponential extrapolation reaches − 646 % -646\% improvement at δ = 0.06 \delta=0.06 . ZNE is worse than the raw estimate on 38–63% of instances. Its extrapolated output is unconstrained: one n = 12 n{=}12 instance reaches error 371 in observable units, three orders of magnitude above the largest raw error in that cell. The median-preserving, tail-growing response also defines the attack surface for A2.

sections.heading: Physical-range safeguards.
sections.text: For our normalized observable, the ideal value lies in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . Clipping an estimate a a to Π [ − 1 , 1 ] ​ ( a ) \Pi_{[-1,1]}(a) cannot increase its absolute error against such a target and caps that error at 2. Thus the error of 371 diagnoses an unconstrained estimator, not an unavoidable property of ZNE. The tables and curves use the original unconstrained fits; neither clipped estimates nor physically constrained fits were evaluated. Their failure rates and mean errors cannot be inferred from these summaries. Appendix F states the bound and the comparison needed to assess these safeguards. NEM, by contrast, tracks CDR at small δ \delta ( + 82 % +82\% versus + 83 % +83\% mean at δ = 0 \delta=0 ) at 1 / 32 1/32 of the quantum cost. Its improvement then declines smoothly to + 44 % +44\% at δ = 0.08 \delta=0.08 , as the high-dimensional oscillatory component of the coherent bias exceeds what the network can learn from 4,000 samples. CDR, which re-fits per instance, stays at 69–86%. Across all 2,000 structured-regime test instances (4–20 qubits), the largest observed neural-corrector error is below the largest raw error in every cell. This is an empirical result, not a formal output bound. A safeguard tightens the observed result. We train three seeds and return the raw value when they disagree beyond a threshold calibrated on unlabeled data. sections.heading: 6.3 Real-hardware validation
sections.text: We next test whether the simulated failure pattern appears on a real device. The experiment uses hardware-efficient VQE on ibm_marrakesh , a 156-qubit Heron r2 processor, with four qubits and two circuit depths. We compare raw execution with folding ZNE under the equal-online-budget protocol using ten and eight instances, 8,192 shots, and one batch. No additional noise is injected. Figure 4 shows the result. Mean ZNE error is 3.0 × 3.0\times the raw error at two layers and 4.1 × 4.1\times at five layers; ZNE is worse on 80% and 88% of instances, respectively. This small study reproduces the direction and tail pattern seen in simulation. It does not isolate control offset from other hardware effects, and its sample size is too small for a broad hardware claim. Repeated calibrations, qubit subsets, and devices are left to future work. This run is not a hardware-accuracy result for the learned corrector. A twin-trained model does not transfer to these near-shot-noise-floor circuits, as detailed in Appendix C . The negative transfer result limits the deployment claim and motivates on-device adaptation [ 22 , 1 ] . Figure 4: Folding ZNE on real hardware ( ibm_marrakesh , 4 qubits): per-instance absolute error for the raw estimate (grey) and ZNE-Richardson (orange); dashed lines are means. In this one-batch study, ZNE is worse on 80% (2 layers, 10 instances) and 88% (5 layers, 8 instances), with mean error 3.0 × 3.0\times / 4.1 × 4.1\times above the raw level.

sections.heading: 6.4 Scaling, controls, and the model’s attack surface
sections.text: Separately trained models maintain their simulated improvement from 4 to 20 qubits (Figure 5 and Table 3 ). Mean error reduction is 72–85% under coherent miscalibration and 61–68% in the stochastic-correlated proxy. This is a per-size scaling study, not cross-size generalization. At n = 16 n{=}16 and n = 20 n{=}20 , NEM matches CDR under miscalibration at 1 / 32 1/32 of CDR’s online executions. Under purely stochastic noise, improvement is smaller ( + 7 +7 to + 22 % +22\% ) as the raw estimate approaches the shot-noise floor.

sections.heading: Direct prediction.
sections.text: Is the network mitigating, or memorizing the expectation-value landscape? A control with identical architecture but no access to the noisy measurement answers this: it is worse than unmitigated execution by 57 57 – 927 % 927\% at every size and regime (Table 3 ). The network’s role is correction, not regression of ⟨ H ⟩ ideal \langle H\rangle_{\mathrm{ideal}} from circuit parameters.

sections.heading: Features.
sections.text: Table 7 isolates what the network uses at n = 8 n=8 . Removing device features triples MAE, while removing circuit features changes it by only 0.3 % 0.3\% . With both groups removed, the measurement-conditioned model still improves over the raw estimate by 46%. The same dependence defines the A1 attack surface. Capacity is not decisive: an 88K-parameter model matches the 428K model ( + 81.4 % +81.4\% versus + 81.7 % +81.7\% ).

sections.heading: Claims and non-claims.
sections.text: At the same online budget, single-execution learned correction occupies the low-budget end of the accuracy–cost frontier after its offline cost is amortized. CDR is more accurate when its 32 executions per target are affordable. The network is a plain residual MLP, and its favorable worst-case behavior is empirical rather than certified. Our security experiment is likewise scoped: it is a white-box metadata stress test within the modeled feature range, not evidence that current cloud calibration APIs have been compromised.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The evaluation is primarily in simulation. The hardware study has only ten and eight instances from one batch, and the twin-trained corrector does not transfer without on-device adaptation (Appendix C ). The noise models are not device-fitted, observables are diagonal, each model is trained for one device family and regime, and the ansatz family is fixed. We also report paired t t -tests from the original evaluation; future work should add repeated hardware calibrations and nonparametric confidence intervals for heavy-tailed cells. The metadata budget is not calibrated to observed device drift: an in-range perturbation need not be small or physically realizable. Matched-budget random perturbations and drift-calibrated budgets remain unevaluated. Best-validation-seed selection also leaves the stability of gains across all training seeds unresolved. If changing calibration requires retraining, the amortization period restarts and adaptation costs must be added before claiming a deployment advantage.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Mitigation methods should be compared under a fixed online budget and with their offline assumptions visible. Under that accounting, ZNE can amplify tail error while leaving the median nearly unchanged. A learned corrector can be useful after training is amortized, but its hardware transfer remains unresolved. Treating provider calibration as execution-unbound input also exposes a concrete metadata attack surface. These results motivate evaluations that report cost, tail risk, and calibration integrity together.

sections.text: Section 6.3 reports the ZNE pattern on ibm_marrakesh and notes that a twin-trained corrector does not transfer. We give the full result here because the negative transfer identifies a limit of simulation-trained mitigation and a benign analogue of A1. The sim-to-real protocol reads the runtime Target , builds an Aer noise model with NoiseModel.from_backend , trains on that digital twin, and tests on the processor. No device data enters training. The twin overstates the observed bias, so the learned correction is too aggressive: improvement is − 3 % -3\% at two layers and − 94 % -94\% at five layers. In simulation, training and test share one noise process; on hardware, the twin overstates the observed bias and the model overcorrects. Closing the gap requires on-device data, label-free augmentation [ 22 ] , or adaptive per-circuit conditioning [ 1 ] .

Our reported aggregate tables are insufficient to reconstruct those paired outputs. Consequently, this version provides the bound, not a new empirical clipping result. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.38713v1 [quant-ph] 30 Sep 2026 \workshoptitle Secure and Trustworthy Quantum Machine Learning (SaTQuML) When Error Mitigation Makes Things Worse: Budget-Aware Evaluation, Extrapolation Failure, and the Calibration Trust Boundary Guilin Zhang Kai Zhao Xiquan Cui Affiliation: Henry Heng Xu Chu Aletta Johanna Blanken Affiliation: Workday AI Research Abstract Error mitigation is expected to turn noisy quantum measurements into more useful estimates. We show that it can instead amplify error. Under control-offset miscalibration, the evaluated unconstrained zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) estimators are worse than no mitigation on 38–63% of simulated instances and produce extreme tail errors. A small IBM Heron study finds worsening on 80–88% of 18 instances across two depths, with mean error 3.0 3.0 – 4.1 × 4.1\times the raw error. In simulation, the median changes little, so median-only monitoring misses the failures. We then compare methods at the same online shot budget per evaluation and report offline training cost separately. After that cost is amortized, a budget-conditioned neural corrector occupies the low-budget end of the simulated accuracy–cost frontier and falls back to the raw estimate when an ensemble disagrees; its hardware transfer remains unsuccessful. Finally, we treat provider-reported calibration as an input that is not bound to the execution-time device state. A white-box projected-gradient stress test on this metadata increases the corrector’s error 8.1 × 8.1\times within the feature ranges used for training and evades the disagreement monitor on half of the worsened cases. Together, the results connect budget-aware evaluation, tail risk, and calibration integrity in near-term quantum learning pipelines. 1 Introduction Variational quantum algorithms such as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are leading candidates for near-term quantum advantage, but their expectation-value estimates are biased by device noise [ 24 , 9 , 4 , 28 ] . Error mitigation aims to remove this bias without the qubit overhead of error correction [ 27 , 7 ] , and in practice it is the component that quantum machine learning pipelines trust to turn noisy hardware output into usable numbers. The most widely used technique, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), amplifies noise by gate folding and extrapolates the measurements back to the zero-noise limit [ 27 , 20 , 14 , 16 ] . Learning-based methods such as Clifford data regression (CDR) instead fit a noisy-to-ideal map on classically simulable circuits run on the same device [ 11 , 26 ] . This paper examines that trust from two directions that are often studied separately. The first is reliability : does a corrected answer improve on the raw one at an affordable quantum budget, and how badly does it fail when its assumptions break? The second is security : what information does the mitigation layer trust, and how can an adversary manipulate it? On reliability, the usual comparison hides a first-order distinction. Methods are compared at a fixed, generous number of shots per circuit execution , yet they need very different numbers of executions per estimate: ZNE three to five, CDR more than thirty per target circuit, a neural model trained offline exactly one. Inside a VQA loop that evaluates thousands of parameter settings under a per-iteration shot budget, these multiplicities decide which method is usable, not the accuracy at unlimited shots. Bultrini et al. [6] made the budget axis explicit for classical methods; we extend it to learned mitigation and make the budget an input of the model itself. Figure 1 summarizes the study. We contribute three pieces of evidence. First, we map the tail-risk boundary of ZNE under coherent offset error and reproduce the failure pattern in a small real-hardware study. Second, we compare raw execution, learned correction, ZNE, and CDR at the same online shot budget, while keeping the learned model’s offline simulation cost visible. Third, we formalize provider-reported calibration as an execution-unbound input and evaluate a projected-gradient metadata attack. The learned corrector is a test case rather than an architectural contribution: CDR remains more accurate when its larger online budget is affordable. Figure 1: Study design. Four mitigation pipelines share one online shot budget and a frozen noise snapshot. Three simulated regimes and a small IBM Heron run support the accuracy–cost, ZNE tail-risk, and metadata-attack analyses. 2 Related work Classical mitigation. ZNE [ 27 , 20 ] assumes the bias varies smoothly with a controllable noise-scale factor; digital implementations amplify noise by unitary folding [ 14 ] , with headline demonstrations at the 100-qubit scale [ 16 ] ; its reliability, however, is contingent on the extrapolation ansatz matching the actual noise response, a sensitivity we quantify in Section 6.2 . Probabilistic error cancellation and virtual distillation trade unbiasedness or stronger suppression for exponential sampling or additional quantum cost [ 27 , 30 , 15 , 17 ] . CDR [ 11 ] fits a linear noisy-to-ideal regression on near-Clifford circuits executed on the device, paying tens of executions per target circuit but inheriting robustness to noise structure because it calibrates on the device as it actually is; Strikis et al. [26] extend the idea with learning-based protocols. Bultrini et al. [6] show that low-cost methods win at small total shot budgets, while data-hungry methods win at large budgets. Our protocol builds on that observation. Learned mitigation. Neural networks have been used to reconstruct observables from noisy quantum data [ 29 ] , mitigate errors in quantum simulation [ 3 ] , and predict ideal expectation values from noisy values and circuit structure [ 21 , 8 ] . Noise-agnostic [ 22 ] and per-circuit-adaptive [ 1 ] variants have also been validated on small hardware experiments. Prior work rarely places learned mitigation and classical baselines on the same online shot budget, and the integrity of calibration inputs remains underexplored. We focus on those two gaps. Quantum computing security. A growing literature attacks quantum computing at the hardware and controller layers: crosstalk-based fault injection in multi-programmed NISQ devices [ 2 ] , crosstalk side channels that reveal a co-tenant’s circuit [ 10 ] , and power side channels on classical controllers [ 12 ] . Adversarial robustness of quantum classifiers has been studied at the model level [ 23 ] . Blind and verifiable quantum computation addresses delegated computation cryptographically [ 5 , 13 ] , although its costs remain impractical for NISQ clouds. We study the classical mitigation layer between these settings and the execution-unbound calibration metadata it consumes. 3 Threat model: provider calibration as a trust boundary Error mitigation is usually analyzed as a numerical problem. In a cloud pipeline it is also security-relevant because the user cannot independently verify the execution-time device state. Provider-reported calibration is authenticated as provider data, but it is not cryptographically bound to the physical process that produced a particular set of counts. We therefore treat it as a trust boundary and study how reliability failures transfer to an adversarial setting. Setting. A mitigated pipeline spans three parties: the user , who compiles circuits and performs classical post-processing; the provider , who executes them on a typically multi-tenant QPU and publishes gate errors, T 1 / T 2 T_{1}/T_{2} , readout asymmetries, and drift statistics; and co-tenants on the same device. The user cannot independently verify the measured counts at scale or confirm that the published snapshot describes the device during execution. Blind and verifiable quantum computation [ 5 , 13 ] address a different integrity problem and remain impractical for the NISQ setting considered here. The boundary. Each mitigation method trusts information that the user cannot independently verify. ZNE assumes folding scales the relevant device noise, CDR assumes its near-Clifford circuits sample the same channel as the target, and a learned corrector consumes published calibration directly as features 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} . The dependencies differ, but all sit below the user’s line of visibility. A1: Calibration spoofing. A dishonest or compromised provider, or an attacker in the metadata path, falsifies calibration while executing circuits honestly. Against NEM this is direct input poisoning. The feature ablation of Section 6.4 shows that removing 𝐱 n \mathbf{x}_{n} triples MAE, so the controlled features are also the ones the model relies on. The sim-to-real study of Appendix C is a benign preview: a model trained under mischaracterized calibration overcorrects by 94% at five layers. A2: Mitigation-aware coherent bias injection. An adversary with access to a calibration routine or controller [ 12 ] can choose a control offset δ \delta to increase post-mitigation error. Section 6.2 sweeps δ \delta over the range used by our noise model. For ZNE, mean error grows and 38–63% of instances become worse, while the median remains near the raw baseline. A median-only dashboard would miss this tail. The small hardware run in Section 6.3 shows that the same failure pattern can arise from ordinary device behavior, without deliberate injection. A3: Co-tenant crosstalk adversaries. The device-layer literature demonstrates that a co-tenant can inject faults [ 2 ] and observe side channels [ 10 ] through crosstalk on multi-programmed hardware. Our stochastic-correlated regime is an illustrative proxy for this setting, not a calibrated reproduction of a specific attack. In that proxy, ZNE is worse than the raw estimate on 44–61% of instances, while the learned corrector improves the mean by 61–68% (Table 5 ). Fail-safe posture and detection. The learned model predicts a residual correction rather than an extrapolated observable. Its outputs are not formally bounded, but the largest observed errors remain below the raw worst case in every evaluated cell. A seed-ensemble disagreement rule adds a zero-quantum-cost monitor: large disagreement returns the raw value. This is an empirical safeguard, not a robustness guarantee. A PGD attack on the calibration channel. We test A1/A2 directly. Holding the measurement and circuit features fixed, we run projected gradient descent on the five calibration features inside an L ∞ L_{\infty} ball equal to half of each feature’s training range. On miscal n = 8 n{=}8 (150 instances), the attack raises mean error from 0.008 to 0.067 and worsens every correction (Table 6 ). At a threshold set to the 95th percentile of clean disagreement, the monitor flags half of these cases. The result is a white-box stress test of the modeled metadata range. Black-box transfer, detector-aware attacks, and empirical calibration tolerances are left to future work. 4 Budget-conditioned neural mitigation A VQA prepares | ψ ( 𝜽 ) ⟩ = U ( 𝜽 ) | 0 ⟩ ⊗ n \left|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\rangle=U(\boldsymbol{\theta})\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes n} and estimates the objective C ( 𝜽 ) = ⟨ ψ ( 𝜽 ) | H | ψ ( 𝜽 ) ⟩ C(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\left\langle\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right|H\left|\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right\rangle . On hardware one observes an S S -shot estimate of the noisy expectation, ⟨ H ⟩ ^ noisy = ⟨ H ⟩ ideal + δ ⁡ ( 𝜽 , ℰ ) + ε S , \widehat{\langle H\rangle}_{\mathrm{noisy}}\;=\;\langle H\rangle_{\mathrm{ideal}}+\delta(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathcal{E})+\varepsilon_{S}, (1) where δ \delta is the bias induced by the noise process ℰ \mathcal{E} and ε S \varepsilon_{S} is measurement noise with scale proportional to 1 / S 1/\sqrt{S} . At the same online budget, single-execution learned correction occupies the low-budget end of the accuracy–cost frontier after its offline cost is amortized. CDR is more accurate when its 32 executions per target are affordable. The network is a plain residual MLP, and its favorable worst-case behavior is empirical rather than certified. Our security experiment is likewise scoped: it is a white-box metadata stress test within the modeled feature range, not evidence that current cloud calibration APIs have been compromised. Limitations. The evaluation is primarily in simulation. The hardware study has only ten and eight instances from one batch, and the twin-trained corrector does not transfer without on-device adaptation (Appendix C ). The noise models are not device-fitted, observables are diagonal, each model is trained for one device family and regime, and the ansatz family is fixed. We also report paired t t -tests from the original evaluation; future work should add repeated hardware calibrations and nonparametric confidence intervals for heavy-tailed cells. The metadata budget is not calibrated to observed device drift: an in-range perturbation need not be small or physically realizable. Matched-budget random perturbations and drift-calibrated budgets remain unevaluated. Best-validation-seed selection also leaves the stability of gains across all training seeds unresolved. If changing calibration requires retraining, the amortization period restarts and adaptation costs must be added before claiming a deployment advantage. 8 Conclusion Mitigation methods should be compared under a fixed online budget and with their offline assumptions visible. Under that accounting, ZNE can amplify tail error while leaving the median nearly unchanged. A learned corrector can be useful after training is amortized, but its hardware transfer remains unresolved. Treating provider calibration as execution-unbound input also exposes a concrete metadata attack surface.
